And according to a GAO, the Accountability Office, they gave us a report last fall, and it said that the USDA headquarters is only using 11% of their in-person office. So I read that report to Secretary Vilsack. He immediately bristled up. He got very defensive and said, oh, are you accusing my workers of not working? And I said, well, I'm not. I'm personally not. I'm just reading what the Government Accountability Office is saying. So Secretary Vilsack denied this trend at this committee hearing. But I had heard from a supervisor at the USDA who anonymously contacted my office and he compared his experience at the agency in Washington DC to a ghost town. And he said there are many emails and phone calls that are simply not being answered because people are not at work. So we've got to get all these bureaucrats back into the office and being responsive to the constituencies that they represent.

turn_text: Senator Ernst, I understand that as we celebrated national agriculture day recently, you want to step further to celebrate women in agriculture. Congratulations.

Oh, thank you and I appreciate that. Yes, so this last week we celebrated National Women in Ag Day and I am very proud that my effort passed the Senate unanimously and I'm grateful for the support of all of our female senators. They all signed on as co-sponsors. And the effort was led by myself and Senator Tina Smith, a Democrat coming from Minnesota. And the resolution honors a million women nationwide. And we have nearly 50,000 of those wonderful women in ag in Iowa alone. So what we are attempting to do is, of course, recognize women in AG, but encouraging the next generation of women.
